drills.q: Which three properties make rendering the workload it is?
options: Huge, deadlined, and independent
Huge, sequential, and latency sensitive
Small, deadlined, and repetitive
Huge, deadlined, and shared
drills.why: The third one is the rare property. Almost nothing else in this handbook has it, and everything about the machine is built on it.

drills.q: How many pixels does a 3840 by 2160 display produce at 120 frames a second?
options: Just under a billion per second
About eight million per second
About a hundred million per second
About ten billion per second
drills.why: Eight million per frame, and a hundred and twenty of those a second. The per frame figure is the one people quote and the per second figure is the one that matters.

drills.q: Roughly how long is there per pixel at 4K and 120 hertz?
options: About one nanosecond
About one microsecond
About one millisecond
About ten nanoseconds
drills.why: The frame budget is 8.333 milliseconds spread over eight million pixels. On a five gigahertz core, a nanosecond is five clock cycles.

options: The ratio of fragments produced to pixels finally shown
Drawing outside the bounds of the display
The extra work of drawing at a higher resolution than the display
Redrawing the frame when it misses its deadline
drills.why: Geometry is submitted before anything knows what will be visible, so a pixel is written, covered, and covered again.

drills.q: What is a typical opaque overdraw factor?
options: Two to four, with transparency pushing local regions to ten or more
Exactly one, because a depth test prevents the rest
Around one hundred
It depends only on the resolution
drills.why: A depth prepass and hierarchical depth testing cut it, and they do not remove it. Take three as a working figure and the work triples before a shader has run once.

drills.q: Why is texture filtering fixed function silicon rather than shader code?
options: It is around 190 billion filtered reads a second, each needing address arithmetic, decode and a blend tree
Shader cores cannot do the arithmetic it requires
It has to happen before the shader runs
It is patented, so it lives in a separate unit
drills.why: Nobody executes that as instructions. It is a pipelined array producing a result per clock, and it has been separate silicon since the beginning.

drills.q: Framebuffer traffic alone, at 4K and 120 hertz with three times overdraw, is roughly what?
options: Tens of gigabytes per second, with no texture traffic counted at all
A few hundred megabytes per second
A few gigabytes per second
Over a terabyte per second
drills.why: Around twelve bytes per fragment for the depth read, depth write and colour write. It is why lossless depth and colour compression is mandatory hardware rather than a refinement.

drills.q: Why are mobile graphics architectures different?
options: A phone has a small fraction of the memory bandwidth and shares it with the processor
Phones do not need a depth buffer
Phone displays refresh too slowly to matter
Mobile shaders are written in a different language
drills.why: Hundreds of gigabytes a second is what makes the immediate mode approach work. Without it the architecture has to change, which is where tile based rendering comes from.

drills.q: How far apart are a large processor and a large graphics card in peak arithmetic?
options: Around sixteen times
Around a thousand times
Around a hundred times
They are roughly equal
drills.why: The unfair comparison against a single core loses the argument. A sixteen core machine is about five trillion operations a second against about eighty, and the processor is still hopeless at this job for reasons that are not about arithmetic.

drills.q: A sixteen core five gigahertz processor rendering 4K at 120 hertz has how many cycles per pixel?
options: About eighty, across all cores
About five, across all cores
About a thousand
About eight hundred
drills.why: 666 million core cycles in a frame, over eight million pixels. With three times overdraw that is twenty seven cycles per fragment.

drills.q: Why does one filtered texture read not fit in twenty seven cycles?
options: It is four dependent loads, each paying a full cache or memory latency, plus the blending
The filtering arithmetic alone exceeds the budget
It needs a system call
The texture must be decompressed first
drills.why: Dependent loads do not overlap. One sample spends the whole per fragment budget, and a real shader wants eight of them.

drills.q: Why is a processor's cache hierarchy the wrong shape for rendering?
options: It optimises one thread's next access and pays for coherence, where a renderer wants aggregate throughput with almost no reuse or sharing
Its caches are too small to hold a framebuffer
It cannot prefetch two dimensional patterns at all
Rendering does not use memory enough to benefit
drills.why: No two fragments share data, so the coherence protocol is pure cost here.

drills.q: How does a processor hide memory latency, and why is that the wrong mechanism here?
options: Out of order execution over one instruction stream, when a renderer already has millions of independent streams waiting
By prefetching, which graphics workloads defeat
By using larger caches, which are too expensive at this scale
By running at a higher clock, which costs too much power
drills.why: An enormous transistor investment to find a handful of independent instructions inside a sequence written to be sequential. The right answer here is to keep hundreds of streams resident and switch between them for nothing.

drills.q: What does deadlined mean for this workload?
options: A frame that misses its slot is a stutter somebody sees, so late is the same as wrong
The work must complete before the next input arrives
The deadline is a target rather than a requirement
Frames are dropped in advance when the load is high
drills.why: Missing by a little is the whole problem. At 120 hertz a frame that takes nine milliseconds instead of eight is not eleven percent worse; it is a dropped frame.

drills.q: Why can a processor not simply be given more cores for this?
options: The per pixel cycle budget is what is short, and each core also spends tens of instructions on what is fixed function elsewhere
Rendering cannot be parallelised across cores
Memory bandwidth is the only limit, and cores do not change it
Cores cannot be added without lowering the clock
drills.why: More cores raise the cycle budget linearly and do nothing about the other three reasons, which is why the answer was a different machine rather than a bigger one.
